name: Anna (prophetess, daughter of Phanuel)
title: The Prophetess Anna – Witness to the Messiah in the Temple
summary: In the infancy narrative of Luke's Gospel, we meet an elderly prophetess named Anna, daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. She had been married only seven years when her husband died, and she then chose to devote her life completely to God through service in the temple in Jerusalem, with fasting and prayer day and night. When she was 84 years old, Joseph and Mary came to the temple with the child Jesus to present him to the Lord according to the regulations of the Mosaic Law. At the moment Simeon finished his prophetic word over the child, Anna stepped forward, praised God, and testified about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. In this way, she became among the very first to publicly proclaim that the Messiah had come. That she belonged to the tribe of Asher—one of the northern tribes scattered after Assyria's conquest in 722 BC—underscores that God's salvation applies to all Israel, not just Judah. Anna is the only woman in the New Testament explicitly called a prophetess, and together with Simeon she represents the faithful remnant in Israel: those who held fast to the promises and in patient expectation saw their fulfillment.

keyEvents.title: Anna's Life as a Widow and Service in the Temple
keyEvents.description: Anna, daughter of Phanuel from the tribe of Asher, became a widow after seven years of marriage. She then devoted her life to serving God in the temple in Jerusalem, where she served with fasting and prayer day and night. At the time of Jesus' presentation in the temple, she was 84 years old.

keyEvents.title: Prophetic Testimony about the Child Jesus
keyEvents.description: When Mary and Joseph brought the child Jesus to the temple to present him to the Lord according to the Law of Moses, Anna stepped forward at the very moment Simeon prophesied over the child. She praised God and spoke about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem, thus becoming one of the very first to publicly testify that the Messiah had come.

versions.summary: Anna was a highly respected prophetess from the tribe of Asher who spent most of her life in the temple in Jerusalem. She was present when the child Jesus was brought to the temple, and she testified about him as the Messiah to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
versions.title: The Faithful Prophetess in the Temple
versions.reason: [critical] Lifespan is set to 'approx. 14 BC - approx. 30 AD', which gives about 44 years, but the text in Luke 2:36-37 states that Anna was 84 years old (or had been a widow for 84 years) when she met the child Jesus. Jesus was born around 4-6 BC, and the presentation at the temple occurred about 40 days later. If Anna was 84 years old at this time, she would have been born around 90-88 BC. The lifespan should be adjusted accordingly.; [minor] Anna is described not only as a prophet but also as one who served God with fasting and prayer night and day in the temple. The role 'widow' or 'worshiper' could be added to provide a more complete picture.; [minor] The last two events ('Meeting the child Jesus at the temple' and 'Prophetic testimony about the Messiah') both refer to Luke 2:38 and practically describe the same moment. They can usefully be merged into one event, or the final event could be expanded with verses 38-40 for better contextualization.; [minor] Luke 2:36 mentions that Anna was married for seven years before her husband died. Although the husband's name is unknown, the spouse field should reflect that she was married, for example with 'unknown' rather than null.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a profile on Anna, there are several interesting aspects to cover: the tribe of Asher and its significance, the textual-critical debate over whether she was 84 years old or had been a widow for 84 years, and her role as one of very few female prophets mentioned in the NT.; [minor] The phrasing 'redemption of Jerusalem' is correct, but it can be clarified that the Greek text uses 'lytrōsis' (redemption/deliverance) for Jerusalem, which carries messianic connotations.

versions.summary: Anna, daughter of Phanuel from the tribe of Asher, is a remarkable figure in the infancy narrative of the Gospel of Luke. After only seven years of marriage, she became a widow and chose to devote the rest of her life to God in service at the temple in Jerusalem, where she worshiped with fasting and prayer day and night. When Joseph and Mary brought the child Jesus to the temple to present him to the Lord in accordance with the Law of Moses, Anna stepped forward – at the very moment Simeon concluded his song of praise – and glorified God. She bore witness about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. In this way, she became one of the very first to publicly proclaim Jesus' messianic identity. The fact that she belonged to the tribe of Asher, one of the northern tribes scattered after Assyria's conquest, underscores that God's plan of salvation encompassed all Israel. Anna is the only woman in the New Testament explicitly referred to by the title prophetess, and together with Simeon she represents the faithful remnant who patiently waited to experience the fulfillment of God's promises.

Based on her being about 84 years old at Jesus' presentation in the temple (around 5–4 BC), her birth would have occurred around 88–89 BC. A clearer formulation would be "ca. 88 BC – unknown".; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically sound. However, the two previous versions had very similar introductions. To ensure further variation, the opening could be rephrased somewhat.; [minor] The role "worshipper" could be clarified to "temple servant" or similar, since Anna did not merely worship in general but had a specific service connected to the temple involving fasting and prayer day and night.

footnotes.text: Anna belonged to the tribe of Asher, one of the ten northern tribes that were scattered after Assyria's conquest of the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC. The fact that a woman from this tribe is identified in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus testifies that some from the northern tribes preserved their tribal identity through the centuries, possibly through return to Judah after the exile or through settlement in Jerusalem in connection with temple service.

The Greek word 'prophētis' (προφῆτις) used for Anna in Luke 2:36 is the feminine form of 'prophētēs'. In the Old Testament, several women are referred to as prophetesses (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Noadiah, and Isaiah's wife), but Anna is the only woman who explicitly bears this title in the New Testament.

There is a textual critical debate over whether Anna was 84 years old or had been a widow for 84 years. The Greek syntax in Luke 2:37 can be interpreted either way. If she had been a widow for 84 years (married at about 14 and widowed at about 21), she would have been over 105 years old. Most scholars interpret the text to mean that she was 84 years old.

Anna's continuous presence in the temple with fasting and prayer reflects a Jewish piety tradition in which elderly widows devoted themselves to service at the sanctuary. In Jewish tradition, widows who lived in celibacy and devotion after their spouse's death were highly respected. This tradition finds resonance in the early church's order for widows (cf. 1 Tim 5:5–10).

The Greek expression 'lytrōsis Ierousalēm' (redemption of Jerusalem) in Luke 2:38 places Anna's testimony in the context of the messianic expectation widespread in Jewish apocalyptic and prophetic thought. The term lytrōsis carries connotations of deliverance and redemption, pointing to the hope for God's intervention to restore his people.

Luke's Gospel consistently highlights women and their role in salvation history. The story of Anna forms a pair with the story of Simeon, and together they serve as male and female witnesses to the identity of the child Jesus—a pattern that may reflect the biblical principle of two witnesses (cf. Deut 19:15).

The name Anna (Hebrew: חַנָּה, Hannah) means 'grace' or 'favor'. It is the same name borne by Samuel's mother in the Old Testament—another devout woman who dedicated her child to the Lord's service in the sanctuary. The similarity in names may be a deliberate literary parallel from Luke's side, drawing lines between Old and New Testament ideals of piety.
